topics.title: Subnetting by hand: five steps
topics.keywords: start beginner maths math calculate network /26 block size

children: Start here · Worked example · IPv4
Let’s work out
without a calculator. We want the network address, broadcast address and usable host range.
Count the bits left for hosts
An IPv4 address has 32 bits. The prefix /26 uses 26 for the network. That leaves
32 − 26 = 6 host bits
Turn the bits into an address count
Each bit has two choices: 0 or 1. Six bits give 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 =
64 addresses
. You can count by doubling: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64.
Find the block containing 42
For this /26, the first three octets stay fixed. The last octet is divided into blocks of 64:
. The number 42 is in 0–63, so the network is
Find the broadcast address
The next network starts at .64. Step back one address:
is the broadcast address of this block.
Leave the endpoints out of the host range
For this conventional subnet, .0 identifies the network and .63 is broadcast. Hosts run from
. That gives
64 − 2 = 62 usable hosts
Network
First host
Last host
Broadcast
The block-size shortcut must follow the octet where the mask changes. A /20 changes in the third octet, not the fourth. And /31, /32 and IPv6 need their own host-count rules.
Standard behind the method:
RFC 4632 — CIDR

topics.title: Bits, bytes and powers of two
topics.keywords: binary beginner maths octet 128 64 32

children: A
bit
is a single 0 or 1. Eight bits form a byte. In an IPv4 address, each of the four dotted numbers is an 8-bit group, also called an
octet
Why does an octet stop at 255?
Eight bits give 2⁸ = 256 different combinations. Counting starts at zero, so the values are 0 through 255.
Convert 42 to binary by hand
128 and 64 are too large: write 0, 0.
Take 32, leaving 10: write 1.
16 is too large: write 0.
Take 8, leaving 2: write 1.
4 is too large: write 0.
Take 2, leaving 0: write 1.
No 1 remains: write 0.
The result is
. To read binary, add the weights under the 1s. To count combinations, double once per bit.

topics.title: From prefix to subnet mask
topics.keywords: binary AND wildcard dotted decimal /26

children: A subnet mask marks network bits with 1 and host bits with 0. A /26 means 26 leading 1s, followed by 6 zeros.
The last octet is 128 + 64 = 192. The mask is
. Its wildcard is the per-octet complement: 255 minus each mask octet, giving
The quick boundary trick
Subtract the changing mask octet from 256:
. Network boundaries occur every 64 in that octet.
Why does address AND mask work?
AND returns 1 only when both input bits are 1. The mask keeps network bits and clears host bits. For .42 in this example:
A valid CIDR mask has a continuous run of 1s, then only 0s. You cannot put another network bit after the host bits start.

topics.title: Cross an octet boundary: /20
topics.keywords: third octet 172.16 4096 larger network calculate

children: Take
. The same method works, but the boundary is in the third octet.
Host bits:
Addresses:
Mask:
255.255.240.0. In the third octet, four network bits give 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 = 240.
Block step:
256 − 240 = 16 in the third octet.
Locate 37:
the third-octet blocks start at 0, 16, 32, 48… so 37 belongs to 32–47.
The last octet varies from 0 to 255 inside this block. An address ending in .0 or .255 is not automatically a network or broadcast address; the prefix determines its role.

topics.title: Choose a prefix for host capacity
topics.keywords: required hosts 50 100 size growth gateway

children: For a conventional IPv4 LAN, choose the smallest power of two that covers the requested hosts plus the network and broadcast addresses.
Example: 50 host addresses
Add the two reserved endpoints: 50 + 2 = 52.
Count powers of two: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64.
32 is too small; 64 fits. 64 = 2⁶, so you need 6 host bits.
Prefix = 32 − 6 =

/27 → 32 total → 30 usable → too small
/26 → 64 total → 62 usable → fits 50
Include router interfaces, printers and other devices in the host requirement. If growth needs 75 hosts, 64 total is insufficient; choose /25 for 126 conventional usable hosts.
This is ordinary IPv4 LAN planning. /31 point-to-point links and cloud-provider reservation policies need different capacity rules.

topics.title: Split a network into equal parts
topics.keywords: FLSM subdivision four subnets /24 /26

children: Every extra prefix bit cuts a block in half. One extra bit gives two child blocks; two extra bits give four.
Example: split 192.168.10.0/24 into four
Four = 2², so borrow 2 more bits for the network. The child prefix is
. Each child has 64 addresses.

Each has 62 conventional usable host addresses. You keep the same total address space, but splitting introduces additional network/broadcast endpoints. Check that your applications have enough host capacity after the split.

topics.title: Glossary and common mistakes
topics.keywords: CIDR subnet prefix gateway broadcast netmask notation errors

children: Subnet / prefix
A contiguous, aligned address block. The number after / says how many leading bits identify it.
Network address
The start of the block, found by setting all host bits to zero.
Broadcast
For a conventional IPv4 subnet, the address with every host bit set to one. IPv6 has no broadcast.
Gateway
A router used to reach destinations via another network. A subnet calculator cannot infer the configured gateway from the address and prefix alone. It is not necessarily the first host.
Common mistakes
Subtracting two from every address count, including IPv6 and /31.
Treating every .0 as a network address and every .255 as broadcast.
Guessing a prefix from an old class A/B/C label.
Calling a covering supernet an exact aggregation.
Assuming an ICMP timeout means the device is offline.

topics.title: Understand an IPv4 subnet
topics.keywords: calculator mask broadcast CIDR hosts

children: A prefix tells you how many bits identify the network. An IPv4 address has 32 bits. With
, 26 identify the network and 6 remain for addresses inside it.

Address count = 2⁶ = 64
Network = 192.168.10.0/26
Broadcast = 192.168.10.63
Host range = 192.168.10.1–192.168.10.62
Conventional usable hosts = 64 − 2 = 62
Read the result
The entered address is 42 addresses after the network boundary. The next /26 begins at
. The /31 and /32 cases follow different rules.
Online reference:
RFC 4632 — CIDR

topics.title: Plan with VLSM
topics.keywords: split allocation host requirements

children: Variable Length Subnet Masking assigns differently sized blocks to networks with different capacity needs. Start with the largest requirement so that small allocations do not fragment the available space.
Example: three networks inside 192.168.10.0/24
Check before allocating
These counts use conventional IPv4 network and broadcast reservations. Include gateways and any spare capacity in your requirement. A cloud provider may reserve additional addresses.
Background:
CIDR address allocation and aggregation

topics.title: Use /31 and /32 correctly
topics.keywords: point to point host route edge cases

children: The usual “subtract two” formula is not universal. A /31 on a point-to-point link uses both addresses. A /32 identifies one address, commonly as a host route.
Example: a point-to-point link

192.0.2.10/31
Endpoint A = 192.0.2.10
Endpoint B = 192.0.2.11
Directed broadcast = Not applicable
Both ends must support /31 operation. A calculator describes the address block; it does not verify how the actual link is configured.
Online reference:
RFC 3021 — IPv4 point-to-point links

topics.title: Understand IPv6 prefixes
topics.keywords: 128 127 64 address format

children: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits wide. IPv6 has no broadcast address, so its capacity display must not subtract two as though it were IPv4.
Example: divide a /48 into /64s

Parent = 2001:db8:1234::/48
Child prefix = /64
Number of child prefixes = 2¹⁶ = 65,536
Addresses in each /64 = 2⁶⁴

This is address-space capacity, not a count of discovered devices or a promise that every address has the same assignability. Link roles and reserved addresses matter. The 2001:db8::/32 prefix is used for documentation.
Online references:
IPv6 addressing
and
IPv6 text formatting

topics.title: Aggregate without extra coverage
topics.keywords: merge supernet range overlap

children: Exact aggregation combines blocks without adding addresses. A covering supernet may also include addresses that were not in the original selection.
Example: adjacent sibling networks
By contrast, the smallest single prefix covering
and
is a /24. That covering block includes 128 additional addresses. Keep the two /26s for an exact result.
Online reference:
CIDR aggregation

topics.title: Read ping and traceroute results
topics.keywords: latency loss jitter timeout diagnostic

children: Ping measures whether a target answers an ICMP echo request and how long the reply takes. A timeout means no reply arrived within the limit; it does not by itself prove that the device is offline.
Example: a short observation

Requests = 100
Replies = 98
Observed reply loss = 2%
Average latency = average of successful replies

Traceroute asks routers along a path to respond. Some routers limit these responses while forwarding traffic normally. Compare intermediate-hop results with the destination before drawing conclusions.
For the proposed jitter display, we will document the exact formula and how missing samples are handled.
Online reference:
Microsoft — ping

topics.title: Interpret a DNS lookup
topics.keywords: records resolver ttl A AAAA MX TXT PTR

children: DNS translates names into records. A records contain IPv4 addresses; AAAA records contain IPv6 addresses. MX records identify mail exchangers, and PTR records are used for reverse lookup.
Illustrative response

Query: host.example — A
Answer: 192.0.2.20
TTL: 300 seconds

The TTL controls how long a response may be cached. Two resolvers can temporarily return different answers because their caches were filled at different times. Distinguish an empty answer, a nonexistent name, a server failure, and a timeout.
Online reference:
RFC 1035 — DNS records and messages

topics.title: IPv6 /127 and /128 in practice
topics.keywords: RFC 6164 point to point single address endpoint

children: IPv6 has no broadcast address. On inter-router point-to-point links, a /127 contains two endpoint addresses. RFC 6164 specifies this use and disables Subnet-Router anycast for the /127 link.
Example: two router interfaces

Network: 2001:db8::10/127
Endpoint A: 2001:db8::10
Endpoint B: 2001:db8::11
Total addresses: 2
Broadcast: Not applicable
A /128 identifies one address, such as
. Neither case uses IPv4’s minus-two formula.
This is a point-to-point link example, not advice to replace ordinary IPv6 LAN /64s with /127s. The prefix math and the link’s configuration requirements are different questions.
RFC 6164 — IPv6 /127 inter-router links

topics.title: The /0 boundary and exact counts
topics.keywords: default route overflow address capacity large IPv6 128

children: A /0 prefix fixes no network bits, so it describes the entire address family. In routing it can be used as a default route. It does not mean that every address can be assigned to hosts.
Exact capacity

A count includes the number of values, not just the highest address. IPv6’s highest address fits in 128 bits; the count 2^128 needs one more bit. The tool must display it exactly and must never try to list every host.
The default route has no previous or next same-size subnet. Arithmetic bounds are not proof of reachability or assignability; the full range includes special-purpose addresses.

topics.title: Read and correct address input errors
topics.keywords: validation leading zeros literal mask scope zone port CIDR prefix input errors

children: An address tells us where; a prefix tells us how much of the address identifies the network. The proposed calculator requires both. It never guesses a prefix from an old address class or looks up a hostname.

Accepted: 192.168.10.42/26
Also accepted: address 192.168.10.42 with mask 255.255.255.192
Correct 192.168.010.42 to 192.168.10.42
Correct 255.0.255.0 to an intended contiguous mask
192.168.10.42 alone still needs a prefix or mask

IPv4 uses four decimal octets from 0 to 255. Leading zeros, hexadecimal and shortened forms are rejected to avoid disagreement between parsers. Mask bits must be consecutive ones followed by consecutive zeros. A wildcard is a different kind of mask and does not belong in the subnet-mask field.

For prefix calculations, enter a plain IPv6 address such as fe80::1 and an explicit prefix. A zone such as %12 identifies an interface for communication; it is not part of subnet arithmetic. The first calculator rejects scoped or bracketed endpoints and ports with an explanation. IPv4-mapped IPv6 remains an IPv6 address.
In the proposed app, incomplete or invalid input makes derived results unavailable. Correct the field before copying or exporting; an old answer must never appear current.
IPv6 addressing syntax — RFC 4291

topics.title: Turn an address range into exact CIDRs
topics.keywords: range CIDR greedy alignment inclusive range cover extra supernet 192.0.2

children: Suppose the required range is 192.0.2.5 through 192.0.2.14, including both endpoints. Subtract the start from the end and add one: 14 − 5 + 1 = 10 addresses.
Begin at the first address. Choose the largest aligned power-of-two block that stays inside the remaining range, then advance to the address immediately after it. Repeat until nothing remains.
Here /31 is an exact set of two addresses. Turning a range into prefixes does not configure point-to-point links or change which addresses may be assigned.

A single covering prefix is 192.0.2.0/28, which contains 16 addresses. It adds six addresses outside the requested range: .0–.4 and .15. Exact conversion and a covering supernet answer different questions; review extra coverage before using a summary route or access rule.
CIDR and route aggregation — RFC 4632

topics.title: Compare two networks in both directions
topics.keywords: compare intersection difference containment overlap union extra missing A B directional

children: Let A be 192.0.2.0/24 and B be 192.0.2.64/26. A has 256 addresses; B has 64. B is entirely inside A.

In both A and B: 192.0.2.64/26 — 64 addresses
In A but not B: 192.0.2.0/26 and 192.0.2.128/25 — 192 addresses
In B but not A: empty — 0 addresses
Check: 64 + 192 = 256
The intersection means addresses shared by both sets. A minus B means what remains after removing B from A. Reversing the inputs reverses the two differences, but leaves the intersection unchanged.

Do not add overlapping input counts before removing duplicates. The union of A and B here is still A, with 256 addresses, not 320. Empty results are valid; a malformed input row is an error and must not silently disappear.
CIDR prefix notation — RFC 4632

topics.title: Plan around pinned networks and gaps
topics.keywords: VLSM pinned reserved fragmentation contiguous aligned deterministic allocation partial

children: A free-address total does not guarantee a requested subnet will fit. The space must also form one correctly aligned block. Existing assignments and pins must remain stable while new requirements are added.

Parent: 192.0.2.0/24
Pinned: 192.0.2.64/26
New LAN for 100 hosts: 192.0.2.128/25 (126 conventional hosts)
New LAN for 50 hosts: 192.0.2.0/26 (62 conventional hosts)

Now pin both .64/26 and .192/26. The free space is .0/26 plus .128/26: 128 addresses in total. A 100-host LAN needs a /25, but neither gap holds one. The correct outcome is an unallocated request with a fragmentation explanation. Moving a pin would change an existing network and is never automatic.

The proposed planner handles larger requests first and uses the lowest aligned free location. Equal-size requests use stored insertion order, so sorting the table or renaming a row does not move networks. Ordinary Allocate preserves existing assignments; a separate reallocation preview is needed to repack movable rows.
If only some requests fit, show the full proposal and every unallocated reason. Applying a partial proposal requires an explicit action. Cancelling leaves the last completed plan intact.
Prefix aggregation and alignment — RFC 4632

topics.title: Read local and external IP addresses
topics.keywords: PC adapters public external IP ipify NAT VPN proxy IPv4 IPv6 scope

children: A PC may have several local addresses at the same time: Ethernet, Wi-Fi, a VPN and virtual adapters can each have IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. There is no single address that describes every connection.

Example local address: 192.168.10.42/26
Network: 192.168.10.0/26
Example scoped endpoint: fe80::42%12
The %12 identifies the interface; it is not a subnet prefix.

The planned My PC & IP view reads addresses and prefix lengths directly from Windows. It keeps address scope separate from assignment states such as preferred, tentative or duplicate. Opening an address in the subnet calculator transfers its address and known prefix, without treating a scope identifier as arithmetic.

Check external IP will contact api.ipify.org for IPv4 and api6.ipify.org for IPv6 over HTTPS, only when requested. The page shows ipify as the provider, separate family results and the observation time. The value means the address seen by that service for that request.

NAT, VPNs and proxies can change the observed external address. It does not prove incoming connections can reach the PC. IPv4 may work while IPv6 fails; a lookup-service failure alone does not prove the Internet is disconnected.
ipify — official API documentation

topics.title: Read adapters, routes and neighbours
topics.keywords: network interfaces routes routing metrics gateway neighbour cache ARP IPv6 interface

children: Start with the adapter: check whether it is operational and has a usable address and prefix. Then inspect the route to the actual destination. The first adapter or first default route in a list is not necessarily the path Windows will choose.

Local address: 192.168.10.42/26
Local prefix: 192.168.10.0/26
192.168.10.50 is inside that prefix.
192.168.10.100 is outside it and needs another applicable route.

Route selection also depends on routes, metrics, source and interface context. Use Route to target to ask Windows about a particular destination. A routing snapshot describes current configuration; it does not prove that the next hop will answer.

The neighbour cache maps locally relevant IP addresses to link-layer information and state. An incomplete or stale entry is not proof that a device is permanently absent. The cache is not a complete network inventory.
The proposed interface, route and neighbour views are read-only. Refresh does not change routes, clear caches or scan the network.
Microsoft — GetBestRoute2

topics.title: Separate TCP connectivity from service health
topics.keywords: TCP connect port handshake refused timeout DNS TLS service health

children: A TCP connection test answers a narrow question: could a handshake complete with this address and port? It does not prove that TLS, authentication or the application protocol will succeed.

Example target: 192.0.2.10, TCP port 443
Connected: the TCP handshake succeeded.
Refused: the connection was explicitly rejected.
Timeout: no successful completion within the deadline.
Refusal can come from a host or network policy; it is not a full application diagnosis. A timeout cannot by itself distinguish filtering, loss, an unreachable path or a silent destination.

If the input is a hostname, show the resolved address and DNS duration separately from TCP connection duration. IPv4 and IPv6 are separate attempts. Do not silently change destination while presenting the run as one measurement.
The proposed test sends no arbitrary application data after connecting. Continue to HTTP/TLS inspection when that is the service being investigated.
Microsoft — TCP connection semantics

topics.title: Inspect HTTP and TLS without hiding failures
topics.keywords: HTTP HTTPS TLS certificate redirect proxy status 401 407 HEAD GET

children: Inspect an explicit URL and method. HEAD requests response headers without a response body; a bounded GET is useful when the server does not implement HEAD as expected. Show the method used, HTTP status, final URL and available timing information.

200: HTTP success for this request; inspect what was actually returned.
301 or 302: a redirect; inspect its destination before following.
401: origin authentication is required.
407: proxy authentication is required.

HTTP success is different from successful TLS validation. The certificate must match the host and satisfy validity and trust checks. Show certificate or revocation errors instead of silently ignoring them.

Redirect following is explicit and bounded. HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrade is rejected. Credentials and cookies are not automatically sent during an unauthenticated diagnostic, and credentials must never follow a redirect to another origin.
Windows versions expose different levels of TLS and phase-timing detail. When a detail is unavailable, the tool should say so rather than infer a protocol or cipher from unrelated settings.
Microsoft — WinHTTP

topics.title: Understand what Wake-on-LAN can prove
topics.keywords: Wake on LAN WoL magic packet MAC UDP port broadcast 102 bytes

children: Wake-on-LAN sends a magic-packet pattern for a specific network adapter's MAC address. The target must already support and be configured for wake-up; the application cannot enable firmware or operating-system power settings remotely.

Magic payload: six FF bytes, followed by the target MAC repeated 16 times.
Each MAC is 6 bytes.
Payload length = 6 + 16 × 6 = 102 bytes.

Choose the destination address, sending interface and UDP port explicitly. The proposed default port is 9. Broadcast forwarding and wake behaviour depend on the network and device configuration; do not assume the packet can cross a router.
A successful send means Windows accepted the datagram for sending. It does not acknowledge receipt or prove the PC woke up. A follow-up ping or connection check is a separate action.
Microsoft — UDP sendto behaviour

topics.title: Calculate MTU probe sizes and interpret silence
topics.keywords: MTU PMTU DF IPv4 IPv6 ICMP payload 1472 1452 packet too big fragmentation

children: MTU measures an IP packet, including its IP header. Ping's data size is only part of that packet. Account for the headers before comparing a probe with an MTU.

Plain IPv4: 1,472 data + 8 ICMP + 20 IPv4 = 1,500 bytes.
Plain IPv6: 1,452 data + 8 ICMPv6 + 40 IPv6 = 1,500 bytes.
IPv4 options or IPv6 extension headers add more bytes.

An IPv4 path-size test must set Don't Fragment and verify the actual behaviour. IPv6 routers do not fragment packets, but the source can: a large Echo Reply alone does not prove an unfragmented packet of that size crossed the path.

If an unfragmented 1,500-byte test succeeds and a 1,501-byte test times out, the result is only a tested lower bound of 1,500. Silence is inconclusive; it is not an exact MTU measurement. A matched packet-too-big response provides different evidence.

The planned tool distinguishes interface MTU, Windows-reported path MTU, tested successful sizes and an observed path estimate. If the backend cannot establish IPv6 source-fragmentation behaviour, it reports that limitation instead of a false exact number.
RFC 8201 — IPv6 Path MTU Discovery

topics.title: Read ping statistics without counting gaps as zero
topics.keywords: ping loss average mean standard deviation p95 variation jitter pending cancelled statistics

children: Use completed eligible probes when calculating Echo reply loss. Pending probes, cancelled work and local send failures must remain visible, but are not evidence of missing network replies.

Four Echo Replies + one timeout + one matched network error = six completed probes.
Echo reply loss = 2 ÷ 6 × 100 = 33.33%.
Pending, cancelled and local errors are listed separately.
Calculate RTT statistics from successful Echo Replies only. A timeout is a gap, never 0 ms or an RTT equal to the timeout setting. Distinguish DNS resolution time from measured Echo RTT.

Successful RTTs: 10, 14, 22, 18 ms.
Minimum 10; mean 16; maximum 22 ms.
Population standard deviation = √20 ≈ 4.47 ms.
Nearest-rank p95 = 22 ms.

RTT variation measures the mean absolute change between successful consecutive probe sequence numbers. A timeout, pause or configuration change breaks the pair. It is not RTP interarrival jitter, which uses a different measurement.

Graph compression must retain timeout/error counts. Resizing or zooming the graph must not change statistics for the same observation window. Intermediate traceroute silence is missing hop responses, not proof of forwarding loss at that router.
RFC 3550 — the distinct RTP jitter definition

topics.title: Web app: install and get started
topics.keywords: PWA install browser iPhone iPad Android desktop Home Screen quickstart Windows

children: Open or install

Open https://velocityeu.github.io/NetTools/app/ while connected to the internet. Installation is optional: the tools also work in a regular browser tab. The web app is a development preview for iOS/iPadOS 17+ and current Android and desktop browsers.

On iPhone or iPad, open the app in Safari, choose Share, then Add to Home Screen. On Android or desktop, use the browser’s Install app or Add to Home Screen option where available. Wording and location vary by browser.
Open Learn and wait for Offline ready before relying on the app without a connection. Keep it open online until the complete offline files have downloaded.
Find your tools
Calculate: enter an IPv4 or IPv6 address and prefix, inspect the network and follow the maths.
Plan: divide a network equally or allocate different-sized networks with VLSM.
Public IP: check the internet-facing IPv4 and IPv6 observations through the labelled ipify service.
Learn: read bundled lessons, inspect offline status and check for updates.
Saved plans: reopen named calculations and plans saved on this device.
Phone, tablet and desktop

On a wide desktop the navigation sits beside the workspace; narrower windows use a horizontal or bottom navigation bar. Inputs and results adapt to the available width. Long result tables may scroll within their panel.
Choose web or Windows

Use the PWA for subnet maths and planning. Use the portable Windows toolkit for local adapter addresses, ping, traceroute, DNS lookup, TCP checks, route and neighbour snapshots, HTTP/TLS inspection, Wake-on-LAN and MTU probing. These native diagnostics are not included in the PWA.

topics.title: Web app: calculations and saved plans
topics.keywords: PWA example IPv4 IPv6 equal split VLSM save draft apply allocation export import backup

children: Calculate an IPv4 subnet
Open Calculate, select IPv4, enter 192.168.10.42/26 and choose Calculate.
Check network 192.168.10.0/26, mask 255.255.255.192, broadcast 192.168.10.63 and conventional host range 192.168.10.1–192.168.10.62.
There are 32 − 26 = 6 host bits, so 2^6 = 64 addresses and 62 conventional usable hosts. Expand the maths and additional details to follow the calculation.
Use Save result to keep a named calculation, or Copy/Share to pass on its text. Unsaved inputs are session-only.
Calculate an IPv6 prefix

Select IPv6 and calculate 2001:db8:1234:5678::abcd/64. The network is 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64, with 2^64 = 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 addresses. IPv6 has no broadcast address; do not apply the IPv4 subtract-two convention. The 2001:db8::/32 prefix is reserved for documentation.
Split a network equally
Open Plan and choose Equal split. Use parent 192.168.10.0/24 and child prefix /26.
For large splits, use the indexed pages and Jump control. Jump uses a zero-based subnet index.
Build a VLSM plan
Choose VLSM with parent 192.168.10.0/24. Add conventional IPv4 LAN requirements for Office (50 hosts), Wi-Fi (25 hosts) and Lab (10 hosts).
Choose Allocate preview. The required sizes are /26 (62 usable hosts), /27 (30) and /28 (14). They occupy 64 + 32 + 16 = 112 addresses before additional reservations.
Review proposed networks and any movement, then choose Apply allocation. If requirements cannot fit, resolve the issue first; an incomplete allocation cannot be applied.
Choose Save plan and supply a name. Use Save draft to keep incomplete requirements for later work.

Pinned assignments retain a specific network; reservations exclude space from allocation. Preserve existing assignments when extending a plan, and review movement before reallocating unpinned networks. Choose point-to-point or host-route semantics explicitly for IPv4 /31 or /32. IPv6 requirements use prefix sizes rather than conventional IPv4 host counts.
Keep a backup

Named plans are stored locally in this browser/device installation, with no account or cloud sync. Use JSON export/import to back them up and move them between PWA installations. Export before clearing browser data or changing devices: browser storage may be cleared or evicted. PWA JSON backups are not compatible with Windows application plan files.

topics.title: Web app: offline, updates and public IP
topics.keywords: PWA offline cache automatic update repair public IP ipify consent privacy recheck

children: Work offline

After Learn shows Offline ready, subnet calculations, planning and bundled lessons work without internet. Public-IP checks and online reference links require a connection. The full website and Windows downloads are outside the app’s offline cache.
Automatic app updates

The PWA checks for updates on launch, on returning to the foreground (checks are throttled to 15 minutes), and every 15 minutes while visible. New files download in the background. An update can activate automatically when all open app tabs are idle and have no unsaved changes.

If work or a dialog prevents activation, the banner offers Update now or Later. Save your work first; Update now may ask you to discard changes or keep working. Save or close other app tabs with unsaved changes too. Learn → Check for updates requests a check manually. App-update checks do not periodically check your public IP.
Recover offline availability
Reconnect and open Learn. Use Check for updates if a newer version may be available.
Use Repair offline cache to verify and restore the complete offline files. If repair cannot finish, save your work, close other app tabs and reopen online.

On the recovery page, try Retry online. Reset installation resets the service-worker registration without deleting saved plans. Browser Clear site data is different and can delete plans; export backups first.
Check your public IP
Open Public IP. The provider is identified as ipify. Start a manual check, or explicitly opt in to checking on launch.
Use Recheck for a fresh observation. IPv4 and IPv6 have separate outcomes and timestamps; there is no periodic public-IP polling.
Read the status as well as the address. A failed refresh can leave a previous observation visible, labelled as previous. Failure of the IPv6 check does not prove your connection has no IPv6.

Requests go over HTTPS to api.ipify.org and api6.ipify.org. The service sees the public address used for that connection. A VPN, proxy or Private Relay may change the observation. This is not your PC’s local adapter address.
Your data
The app has no account, cloud plan sync, analytics or external fonts. Public-IP checks are optional. Copy/Share exports text; subnet inputs are not placed in share URLs.
